_readme: Curated Daily Pick stock. Founder brief, 29 Jul: 'questions should be really tricky
— no basic questions or tips at all. No RC, no long questions. One filter: students
should feel THIS QUESTION IS GOOD, I SHOULD SOLVE THIS. For a tip: YRR I SHOULD TRY
So every question here carries a named TRAP — the plausible wrong answer is in the
options, and the explanation says why it is wrong. A question with no trap is a drill,
not a pick. And every tip is an instruction you could follow in the next hour: a
number, a trigger, or a concrete first move. 'Practise more' is not a tip.
Rendered as CURATED (curated = true), never as a student's words — see
Validated by src/lib/daily-pick-seed.test.ts. Loaded by scripts/seed-daily-pick.mjs.

questions.text: What are the last two digits of 7¹⁰⁵?
questions.explanation: The last two digits of powers of 7 cycle every four: 07, 49, 43, 01. 105 = 4×26 + 1, so it lands on the first entry — 07. Never compute the power; find the cycle length.

questions.text: If log₂x + log₄x + log₁₆x = 7, what is x?
questions.explanation: Put everything in base 2: log₄x = (log₂x)/2 and log₁₆x = (log₂x)/4. So log₂x × (1 + ½ + ¼) = 7 → log₂x × 7/4 = 7 → log₂x = 4 → x = 16. Convert to one base before adding anything.

questions.text: A vessel holds 40 litres of pure milk. 8 litres is drawn out and replaced with water. This is repeated two more times. How much milk is left?
questions.explanation: Each replacement leaves 32/40 = 4/5 of the milk, so after three: 40 × (4/5)³ = 20.48 litres. The trap is subtracting 8 three times to get 16 — after the first round you are removing a mixture, not pure milk.

questions.text: The sum of the first n terms of a sequence is 3n² + 5n. What is its 10th term?
questions.explanation: The nth term is Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ = (300 + 50) − (243 + 45) = 62. The trap is reading 3n + 5 off the formula and answering 35 — that is the answer to a question nobody asked.

questions.text: If x + y = 12 and both x and y are positive, what is the maximum value of x²y?
questions.explanation: Split the sum in the ratio of the powers, x : y = 2 : 1 → x = 8, y = 4 → 64 × 4 = 256. Equal parts (x = y = 6) gives only 216: equal is optimal ONLY when the powers are equal.

questions.text: In a right-angled triangle the altitude to the hypotenuse is 12 cm, and it cuts the hypotenuse into two parts, one of them 9 cm. How long is the other part?
questions.explanation: The altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two segments: 12² = 9 × k → k = 16. One identity settles it; three applications of Pythagoras also work and cost four minutes.

questions.text: The roots of x² − px + q = 0 differ by 1. Which of these must be true?
questions.explanation: (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ = p² − 4q, and the difference is 1, so p² = 4q + 1. The moment a question mentions the DIFFERENCE of roots, reach for (α − β)² — never solve for the roots themselves.

questions.text: A train crosses a pole in 9 seconds and a 240 m platform in 24 seconds. How long is the train?
questions.explanation: The speed is the same in both: L/9 = (L + 240)/24 → 24L = 9L + 2160 → L = 144 m. Crossing a pole covers the train's own length; crossing a platform covers length + platform.

questions.text: An article is marked 60% above cost. What is the largest discount the shopkeeper can offer and still make a 12% profit?
questions.explanation: Take CP = 100 → marked price 160, and the selling price must be 112. Discount = 48/160 = 30%. The trap is computing the discount on the cost price (48/100 = 48%); discount is always on the marked price.

questions.text: For how many positive integers N does N! end in exactly 5 zeros?
questions.explanation: Trailing zeros come from factors of 5. 24! has 4 zeros; 25! has 6, because 25 contributes two fives at once. The count jumps straight from 4 to 6 and skips 5 — so no N works at all.

questions.text:
A, B and C each make one statement, and exactly ONE of them is telling the truth.
A: “B is lying.”
B: “C is lying.”
C: “A and B are both lying.”
Who is telling the truth?
questions.explanation: If A were truthful, B lies → C is truthful → two truth-tellers ✗. If C were truthful, A and B both lie → but A lying means B is truthful ✗. If B is truthful: C lies, and A lies (A said B is lying, which is false) — exactly one ✓.

questions.text: Four cards on a table show A, 5, D and 8. Every card has a letter on one face and a number on the other. To test the rule “if a card has a vowel on one face, it has an even number on the other”, which cards MUST you turn over?
questions.explanation: Turn A (a vowel must have an even number behind it) and 5 (an odd number must not have a vowel behind it). Turning 8 proves nothing — the rule never claims an even number needs a vowel. Test where the rule can FAIL, not where it can be confirmed.

questions.text: A 3×3 grid holds 1–9, each once, so that every row, column and diagonal sums to 15. The centre is 5 and one corner is 2. What sits in the corner diagonally opposite?
questions.explanation: Every line through the centre sums to 15, so a cell and the cell opposite it sum to 10. Opposite 2 is 8. You never need to construct the full square — one property of the centre answers it.

questions.text: In a class of 100 students, 70 passed Maths and 60 passed English. What is the MAXIMUM number who could have failed both?
questions.explanation: At least 70 students passed something, so at most 30 failed both — reached when every English passer also passed Maths. A maximum-neither question is really a make-the-overlap-as-large-as-possible question.

questions.text: Between 3 and 4 o'clock, at what time are the hour and minute hands exactly opposite each other?
questions.explanation: Opposite means a 30-minute gap on the dial: minutes = (5H + 30) × 12/11 = 45 × 12/11 = 540/11 = 49 1/11. One formula, one substitution. Clock questions are only slow if you re-derive them each time.

questions.text: In a 100 m race A beats B by 10 m, and B beats C by 10 m. By how much does A beat C over the same 100 m?
questions.explanation: When A runs 100, B runs 90. When B runs 100, C runs 90 — so when B runs 90, C runs 81. A beats C by 19 m, not 20: the second margin is measured over a shorter distance. Chain the RATIOS, never the margins.

questions.text: Four teams play a single round robin (every pair exactly once). No team plays more than one match per day. What is the minimum number of days needed?
questions.explanation: Six matches, and at most two can run on a day (4 teams, 2 per match) → at least 3 days. Three works: (AB, CD), (AC, BD), (AD, BC). Establish the lower bound first, then construct a schedule that hits it.

questions.text: Three boxes are labelled “Apples”, “Oranges” and “Mixed”. Every label is wrong. You may draw ONE fruit from ONE box. Which box do you draw from to identify all three?
questions.explanation: Draw from “Mixed”. Its label is wrong, so that box is pure — whatever you pull names it. The other two then follow, because their labels must be wrong too. Always start where the wrong label rules out the most.

questions.text: A firm earned ₹100 crore revenue in 2020 against ₹90 crore of costs. Revenue grows 10% a year, costs 5% a year. In which year does annual profit first cross ₹25 crore?
questions.explanation: 2021: 110 − 94.5 = 15.5. 2022: 121 − 99.2 = 21.8. 2023: 133.1 − 104.2 = 28.9 ✓. Profit has no single growth rate of its own — that is exactly why you must step year by year instead of compounding the gap.

questions.text: 100 people stand in a circle numbered 1 to 100. Counting from 1, every second person is eliminated (2, 4, 6 …) and the circle keeps closing until one person is left. Which number survives?
questions.explanation: Take the largest power of 2 below 100 (that is 64) and let L = 100 − 64 = 36. The survivor is 2L + 1 = 73. Worth memorising: the same one-line rule handles any circle size.

questions.text: “Since we launched the app, student dropout has fallen 30%. So the app's reminders are working.” Which assumption does this argument depend on?
options: Students who dropped out never opened the reminders
Nothing else that could affect dropout changed over the same period
Reminders are the most used feature in the app
Dropout is the only meaningful measure of a student's progress
questions.explanation: The argument credits one cause for a change, so it holds only if no rival cause was available. Negate option 2 — “something else did change” — and the conclusion collapses. That collapse test is what identifies an assumption.

questions.text: “Every student who cleared the mock had completed the syllabus.” Which of these MUST be true?
options: Every student who completed the syllabus cleared the mock
A student who did not complete the syllabus did not clear the mock
Completing the syllabus is what causes a student to clear the mock
Most students who cleared the mock studied every day
questions.explanation: Only the contrapositive is guaranteed. Option 1 reverses the statement, option 3 upgrades a pattern into a cause, option 4 invents information. In inference questions the contrapositive is nearly always the safe answer.

questions.text: Complete the paragraph: “For decades cities fought congestion by building wider roads, and every time the traffic came back. The reason is straightforward: ______”
options: drivers naturally prefer wider roads to narrow ones
new road capacity generates journeys that were never made before
public transport is almost always cheaper than driving
congestion has never been measured in a reliable way
questions.explanation: The blank has to explain why extra capacity FAILS, and only option 2 does — the road creates its own new demand. The rest are true-sounding statements answering a different question, which is the standard para-completion trap.

questions.text:
Arrange into a coherent paragraph:
1. But the map had been drawn before the river changed course.
2. The surveyors trusted it completely.
3. In 1897 a single map governed every land claim in the district.
4. Entire families therefore held title to fields that no longer existed.
questions.explanation: 3 must open — it is the only sentence with nothing to refer back to. “it” in 2 needs the map. “But” in 1 introduces the flaw. “therefore” in 4 delivers the consequence. Lock each connector to its antecedent and the order is forced.

questions.text: “A skill practised once a week decays in the gaps between sessions. The same skill practised ten minutes a day compounds. What builds fluency is frequency, not total hours.” Which option best captures this?
options: Long practice sessions are a waste of time
Frequent short practice beats occasional long practice, because fluency is built by frequency
Ten minutes is the ideal length for a practice session
Every skill decays unless it is practised
questions.explanation: A summary has to carry the contrast AND its reason. Option 1 overstates, option 3 invents a prescription, option 4 keeps only half the paragraph. Option 2 is the only one that survives both tests.

questions.text: “Mock scores predict CAT percentile, so a serious aspirant should take one mock every day.” Which option most weakens this?
options: Mock tests from different providers vary in difficulty
A daily mock leaves no time to analyse the mistakes each mock reveals
Some toppers took fewer than twenty mocks in total
Mock tests are expensive for most aspirants
questions.explanation: The conclusion recommends an ACTION, so the strongest attack shows the action defeats its own purpose. Option 3 is an anecdote, option 1 adds noise, option 4 argues cost rather than effectiveness.

questions.text:
Three of these sentences build one argument; one does not belong. Which is the odd one?
1. A language is considered dead once its last fluent speaker dies.
2. Roughly one language disappears somewhere in the world every two weeks.
3. Written records rarely capture how a language was actually pronounced.
4. Half of the world's 7,000 languages may not survive this century.
questions.explanation: 1, 2 and 4 are all about languages dying and how fast. 3 is about the limits of written records — a different subject entirely. Name the shared thread in one word (“extinction”) and the stray becomes obvious.

questions.text: “The library is open only on days when the college is open.” The college was open on Tuesday. What follows?
options: The library was open on Tuesday
The library may or may not have been open on Tuesday
The library was closed on Tuesday
The library is open on every day the college is open
questions.explanation: “Only on” makes the college being open NECESSARY for the library to open, not sufficient — it permits, it does not guarantee. Most students pick option 1, and that single confusion is the entire question.

questions.text: “A study found that people who write their goals down achieve more. Newspapers reported it as proof that writing goals down causes success.” What is the flaw?
options: The study did not include enough participants
People already disposed to follow through are also the people who write goals down
Writing is a slow way of recording a goal
Success is difficult to define precisely
questions.explanation: Self-selection: the two groups already differ before any writing happens, so the writing may be a symptom rather than a cause. Whenever a study compares people who CHOSE a behaviour, ask what else that choice reveals about them.

questions.text: “The minister's answer was studiously ______: it committed to nothing while appearing to promise everything.” Which word fits best?
questions.explanation: “Committed to nothing while appearing to promise everything” is deliberate ambiguity — exactly what equivocal means. Anodyne is bland and inoffensive, laconic is using very few words, and candid is the opposite of what is described.

tips.text: Learn every square up to 30 and every cube up to 15 cold. A surprising share of QA sums collapse the moment you recognise one of them.
Any equation with |x| in it: split at each point where the modulus flips sign, then solve each range separately. There is no shortcut.
For remainder questions, reduce the base before the power. 143 mod 7 is 3, so 143^n becomes 3^n — the big number never has to appear.
Options are data. Plug the middle two options in first: the direction the value moves tells you which half to keep. Two steps, done.
When a sum gives you the 'after' state, work backwards from it. Forward algebra on the same question needs twice as many variables.
Two linear equations, two unknowns: add them, then subtract them. One of those two almost always hands you the answer directly.
Any 'at least one' counting question: count the opposite case (none at all) and subtract from the total. Fewer cases, no double counting.
With a fixed sum, equal parts is NOT always the maximum. Split in the ratio of the powers: x²y peaks at x:y = 2:1, never at 1:1.
In every profit-loss sum, set cost price = 100. Each percentage turns into a rupee figure and the whole chain becomes mental arithmetic.
Put a 90-second ceiling on each QA sum. If it hasn't opened up by then, mark and move — that one habit is worth 3-4 marks on the real paper.
Spend the first 40 seconds turning the set into ONE table, before you read a single question. A set you cannot tabulate is a set to skip.
Hunt for the clue that fixes exactly one cell and start there. Working down the clue list in order is why sets feel like they never close.
Pick sets by how CLOSED they are, not by topic. Exact-value clues mean it will crack; a set built only on 'at least' clues will eat 20 minutes.
When a liar makes a statement, write its negation down as a fact. A lie narrows the possibilities exactly as much as the truth does.
For min/max questions, stop hunting for cases. Push one quantity to its extreme, then check whether every constraint still survives.
Read the whole set once before writing anything. The last line very often deletes half the cases you were about to draw out by hand.
Attempt a 4-question set only if you can see yourself getting 3. Two-out-of-four sets are where DILR scores quietly go to die.
Percentages in a chart usually sit on different bases. Circle what each one is a percentage OF before you compute a single number.
In tournament sets the total points across all teams are fixed. Compute that total first — it caps every individual score immediately.
One clean page per set, and never erase. When you hit a contradiction you need to see which assumption to undo, not a smudge.
Stop hunting for the opening sentence. Find the PAIR that must sit together — two locked sentences usually kill three of the four options.
In inference questions, reject any option containing 'all', 'never' or 'must' unless the passage itself used those words.
'Only if' is not 'if'. A large share of VARC logic questions turn on that one distinction — mark the phrase every time it appears.
Write a five-word summary of each paragraph in the margin as you read. Those words ARE your answer to the main-idea question.
Name the shared thread in ONE word before you look at the options. The stray sentence then stands out in about five seconds.
The trap option is true but beside the point. Ask 'does this answer the question asked?' — never just 'is this statement true?'
Read one editorial a day and write its ARGUMENT in one sentence — not a summary. Six weeks of that moves accuracy more than any book.
When two options say nearly the same thing, the difference between them IS the question. Compare only that difference and ignore the rest.
For assumption questions, negate the option. If the argument falls apart, that was the assumption. If it survives, it never was one.
Keep every new word together with the sentence you met it in. Words learnt inside a sentence stick; the same word on a list does not.
Divisible by 9? Add the digits. 5,832 gives 5+8+3+2 = 18, so yes. The digit sum also gives the remainder on dividing by 9, for any number.
Divisible by 8? Check only the last three digits. For 71,512 the tail 512 is 8 x 64, so the whole number is divisible too. The rest never matters.
Use negative remainders. 99 is -1 mod 100, so 99^51 mod 100 is (-1)^51 = -1, which is 99. Any base next to a round number collapses this way.
Fermat: for a prime p, a^(p-1) leaves remainder 1 (a not a multiple of p). 2^100 mod 7: 100 = 6 x 16 + 4, so it is 2^4 mod 7 = 2.
Sum of factors: for 2^a x 3^b multiply (1+2+...+2^a)(1+3+...+3^b). For 12 = 2^2 x 3 that is 7 x 4 = 28. Listing factors takes longer.
Only perfect squares have an odd number of factors. Every 'which lockers stay open' question is really 'how many squares are there up to n'.
A price rises 25%. To undo it, it must fall 20%, not 25%. Rise by 1/n and the fall that undoes it is 1/(n+1). Same rule in reverse.
x% of y = y% of x. 16% of 25 is 25% of 16, which is 4. Swap them whenever the other way round is easier to do in your head.
Two items sold at the same price, one at x% profit and one at x% loss, always make a net LOSS of x^2/100 percent. At 10% each: a 1% loss.
Marked up m%, then discounted d%: net profit = m - d - md/100. Mark up 50% and discount 20%: 50 - 20 - 10 = 20% profit.
For two years, CI minus SI = P(r/100)^2. On Rs 10,000 at 10% the gap is exactly Rs 100. You never need to compute either interest.
Equal distances at speeds a and b: average speed = 2ab/(a+b), never (a+b)/2. 40 and 60 km/h average 48, not 50. The 50 is always an option.
Trains crossing: add the lengths; add speeds if opposite, subtract if same way. Time = total length / relative speed. That is every train sum.
Boats: downstream = b + s, upstream = b - s. So the boat's speed is the AVERAGE of the two, and the stream's is HALF their difference.
Recurring decimals are infinite GPs. 0.4545... = 45/99 = 5/11. Put the repeating block over as many 9s as it has digits, then simplify.
In an AP, any term is the average of terms equally far either side of it. The 7th term is the average of the 5th and 9th, or the 1st and 13th.
n people round a circular table: (n-1)! ways. For a necklace or garland, which can be flipped over, halve it: (n-1)!/2.
Arrangements of MISSISSIPPI = 11!/(4! 4! 2!). Divide by the factorial of every repeat count; letters, colours or balls, same rule.
n identical items among r people, empty hands allowed: C(n+r-1, r-1). 5 sweets among 3 children: C(7, 2) = 21. No case listing.
Two dice: 36 outcomes, and sum 7 is most likely at 6/36. Sums mirror around 7, so P(sum 5) = P(sum 9) = 4/36. Count one side only.
Any side of a triangle is less than the sum of the other two and more than their difference. Sides 3 and 7: the third lies strictly between 4 and 10.
A regular hexagon of side a is six equilateral triangles: area = (3√3/2)a^2. Split any hexagon question into those six before anything else.
Angle bisector theorem: the bisector from A cuts BC in the ratio AB : AC. Sides 6 and 9 split the base 2 : 3. No trigonometry needed.
Scale every length by k: areas scale by k^2, volumes by k^3. Double a cube's side and its volume is 8 times, not 2. Same for any solid.
a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b). 97 x 103 = 100^2 - 3^2 = 9,991. Two numbers equally far from a round number multiply in one line.
log_a(b) = log b / log a in any base, so log_a(b) x log_b(a) = 1. Most log questions fall apart once every term is in the same base.
AM ≥ GM for positive numbers: (a+b)/2 ≥ √(ab), equal only when a = b. So x + 1/x ≥ 2 for every positive x. Most minimum questions end there.
b^2 - 4ac decides the roots before you solve: positive, two real; zero, one repeated; negative, none real. Many questions ask only this.
Triangle area from coordinates: ½|x1(y2-y3) + x2(y3-y1) + x3(y1-y2)|. If it comes out zero, the three points lie on one line.
Two start towards each other and meet. If after meeting A takes t1 and B takes t2 to finish, their speeds are in the ratio √t2 : √t1.
Skim the opening lines of all four sets before starting any. The easiest set is often the third or fourth; the paper is not in order of difficulty.
Linear seating with some facing north and some south: 'left' flips for the south-facers. Draw an arrow on every person as you place them.
Circular seating facing the centre: a person's left is clockwise. Facing outwards: anticlockwise. Note it in a corner before placing anyone.
A bigger percentage of a smaller base can tie or lose: 40% of 250 and 25% of 400 are both 100. Compare the products, never the percentages.
Adding a long column? Round each value to the nearest 5 or 10 and keep the rounding in a separate tally. Correct once at the end, not per line.
Check the y-axis first. An axis starting at 50 turns a small change into a tall bar. Read the numbers, never the heights.
Two y-axes on one chart: label which series uses which axis before comparing anything. Most wrong options read one series on the other's scale.
Win 2, draw 1, loss 0: every match adds exactly 2 points to the table. Total points = 2 x matches, however the results fall.
3 for a win, 1 for a draw: a decided match adds 3 points, a draw only 2. So draws = 3 x matches - total points. One subtraction.
Minimum wins to qualify? Build the worst case: as many teams as possible tied just above you. The last qualifier often needs fewer wins than it looks.
The smallest possible overlap of A and B is n(A) + n(B) - total, or zero if negative. If 70% like tea and 60% coffee, at least 30% like both.
Clock hands overlap 11 times in 12 hours, not 12. The minute hand gains 5.5° a minute on the hour hand; every clock question starts there.
Day of the week: an ordinary year moves it on by 1, a leap year by 2. 1 Jan 2025 was a Wednesday, so 1 Jan 2026 is a Thursday.
A century year is a leap year only if it divides by 400. 2000 was a leap year, 1900 was not. Calendar sets like to plant this trap.
Flow networks: at every node except the start and the end, what flows in flows out. Any node with one unknown is a single subtraction.
Most non-overlapping meetings? Sort by END time and always take the one that finishes first. That greedy rule gives the maximum every time.
'A only if B' means: A in, so B in; B out, so A out. Nothing follows from B in or A out. Write both arrows before using the clue.
If A says 'B is lying' and B says 'A is lying', exactly one of them is lying. Mark that pair first; it fixes the count of liars quickly.
To let the most people score above X, give everyone else the least they are allowed. The minimum for one group is the maximum for the other.
Pigeonhole: 13 people guarantee two share a birth month. For any 'minimum to be sure' question, build the worst case, then add one.
Five scores average 60 and none is above 70? The lowest is at least 300 - 4 x 70 = 20. Totals turn averages into hard limits.
Stuck between two cases? Answer the questions both cases agree on first. They score the same either way, and the rest may decide the case.
Leaving a set half done is fine. Bank the questions it already answers and move on. Marks are per question, not per completed set.
The average of percentages is not the overall percentage. When the bases differ, recompute from the totals. Options are built from the shortcut.
Weighing puzzles: each weighing has three outcomes, so n weighings separate up to 3^n cases. 9 coins, one heavier: 2 weighings are enough.
On a standard die opposite faces add to 7. Across views, the face that never appears beside X is the one opposite X.
Floors puzzle: the ground floor is 1 unless the set says 0. Write the numbering rule at the top of the page before placing anyone.
Knockout brackets: two players can meet only in the round where their halves of the draw join. Mark the halves before any 'who met whom'.
'Must be true' needs one case that breaks each wrong option. 'Could be true' needs only one case that works. Decide which you are asked.
Timetable sets with am/pm or time zones: convert every time to minutes past midnight on one clock first. Mixed formats are where errors breed.
An option that reuses a passage word in a different sense is a trap. Matching words is not matching meaning. Check the sense, not the spelling.
Strengthen or weaken: find the link between evidence and conclusion. The right option hits that link, not the conclusion on its own.
Tone options are usually moderate. 'Measured scepticism' beats 'outright contempt' unless the author is openly hostile in the passage.
'The author would most likely agree': the answer is one small step from the text. If you need two assumptions to reach it, reject it.
Main idea: reject options that cover more than the passage, or only one paragraph of it. The right one matches the passage's scope exactly.
Dense passage? Slow down on the first paragraph. Once you know the topic and the author's side, the rest reads nearly twice as fast.
When a question quotes a phrase, reread two sentences either side of it. Its meaning depends on what surrounds it, not the phrase alone.
'All EXCEPT' or 'NOT supported': three options are true. Mark T or F against every option before choosing. Your eye wants the true one.
Look for time words: dates, 'first', 'later', 'eventually', 'today'. They often fix the order before meaning does. Circle them first.
General comes before specific. A sentence introducing an idea precedes its example, and 'for instance' never opens a paragraph.
Full name before short name. 'The World Health Organization (WHO)' comes before any sentence that says only 'WHO'. Acronyms lock pairs.
Find the closing sentence as well: 'thus', 'therefore', 'in short' usually end the chain. With both ends fixed, the middle is quick.
Write your own one-line summary before reading the options. Then pick the option closest to yours, not the one that sounds cleverest.
The odd sentence often fits the topic but not the argument. Ask what the paragraph is DOING, not what it is about. The stray one does something else.
When an argument jumps from 'A goes with B' to 'A causes B', the best weakener names another cause. Correlation is where these arguments break.
Paradox questions: the answer explains how both facts can be true at once. An option that denies either fact is wrong, however neat.
An inference must follow from the text alone. If an option needs outside knowledge to hold, however reasonable it sounds, it is not inferred.
Learn roots, not lists: 'bene' good, 'mal' bad, 'chron' time, 'loqu' speak. One root unlocks dozens of words you have never seen.
Two-sense words are favourites: 'sanction' (approve or punish), 'cleave' (split or cling), 'oversight' (supervision or a miss). Check which fits.
Read one long-form essay a day from Aeon, The Atlantic or The Economist. Their argument-heavy style is the closest match to CAT passages.
After any article, ask what the author would say to someone who disagrees. If you can answer in one line, you understood the argument.
Start VARC with the RC you find easiest, not the first on screen. A confident first passage buys time for the hard one.
Never reread a whole passage for one question. Go to the paragraph your notes point to. A full reread costs a question's worth of time.
In mock review, go through the questions you got RIGHT by guessing. They are the errors waiting for you on the real paper.
Down to two options? Pick the one with softer language and fewer claims. It is harder to prove wrong, and CAT keys are defensible by design.
The missing sentence must match the paragraph's tone and tense. An option in the wrong tense or register is out, whatever it says.
Science passages: skip the jargon on the first read. Track only three things: the claim, the evidence, and who disagrees.
Humanities passages hide the author's view in qualifiers: 'arguably', 'perhaps', 'it is tempting to'. Those words mark what the author doubts.
When a passage sets out two views, note which one the author holds. Many options state the view the author rejects, accurately.
A summary keeps the author's stance. If the paragraph is critical, a neutral option that only describes the topic is wrong.
